results.title: Statsig Glossary - Correction For Multiple Comparisons
results.content: # Correction For Multiple Comparisons. Correcting for multiple comparisons becomes essential to maintain the overall desired significance level (e.g., α = 0.05) across all tests. By adjusting the significance threshold for each individual test, we can control the family-wise error rate (FWER) or the false discovery rate (FDR), depending on the correction method used. Implementing multiple comparison corrections ensures the integrity of your experimental results. In practice, the choice of correction method depends on factors such as the number of tests, the desired balance between Type I and Type II errors, and the consequences of false positives and negatives. Limiting the number of comparisons reduces the impact of correction for multiple comparisons. When applying corrections for multiple comparisons, you face a trade-off between false positives (type I errors) and false negatives (type II errors). By being selective and applying appropriate corrections for multiple comparisons, you can strike a balance between controlling error rates and maintaining the power to detect meaningful differences.

This is where we might want to correct our testing process for multiple comparisons, usually by considering a stricter (lower) significance level but this has the disadvantage of reducing our statistical power to detect some real differences! A significance level refers to a value, say α = 0.05, that we use to decide if we should reject a null hypothesis (e.g., no difference in the means between two treatments). One option is to continue using our original significance level, say α = 0.05 for each of the comparisons (that is α = αf). Use an experiment-wise significance level**. In this case we will calculate an appropriate αf (the experiment-wise significance level) based on k tests. This means that for ALL tests we are going to perform, we set a significance level for an individual test that will result in an x 100% error rate (e.g., 5%) in the complete study. If we set our to be 0.05 (5%) then the for a single test changes to 0.0050 and 0.0005 for multiple comparisons on 10 and 15 treatments, respectively. As you can see, now it is a lot harder to report significant results for single test, but on the other hand, we are being careful not to report too many false positives in the complete experiment. The key here is that 1) your focus is on just those pre-planned comparisons 2) these are an integral part of your experimental design and 3) you will not perform additional comparisons (or hypothesis tests) after exploring your data. As each of these pre-planned comparisons represent your real hypotheses of interest, you can always use your predefined significance level with no adjustment. Here you are saying that you are willing to report the comparison of each new formulation against the commercial control with only α × 100% (e.g., 5%) expected false positives. One element to be careful of is that most statistical software will allow you to implement, in just seconds, several of the multiple comparison tests. Finally, you also have to consider that your decision to control or not to control the multiple comparison experiment-wise significance level will likely create some conflict or disagreement between you, other scientists, reviewers and/or your target audience.
